chapterTitle: Advanced Web3 Frontend Integration & Wallet Connect
aiGenerationNote:
Create a 15-minute live coding video. Start with a simple React DApp using `ethers.js` to connect MetaMask and display the user's balance. Then, integrate `Web3Modal` and `WalletConnect`, showing how to connect various wallets (Metamask, mobile wallet via QR). Next, demonstrate an EIP-712 signature, walking through the `domain`, `types`, and `value` objects, and showing the signature prompt in MetaMask. Conclude by adding robust error handling for `insufficient funds` and `user rejected transaction` scenarios, showing how to catch and display user-friendly messages. Use a split-screen view for code and browser/wallet interaction.

---

screens.title: Advanced Web3 Frontend Integration & WalletConnect
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll build a mental model for production-ready Web3 frontends. You will understand when to use a read-only provider versus a signer, how to add multi-wallet support so users can choose MetaMask, a mobile wallet, or hardware device, and why structured signatures like EIP-712 are safer than raw signing. We'll also cover practical patterns: estimating gas to avoid failed transactions, monitoring status until confirmation, and surfacing clear error messages. For example, you might use a BrowserProvider for reads, then obtain a signer when the user needs to submit a payable transaction. WalletConnect acts as a bridge for mobile wallets, enabling QR or deep-link connections instead of a single injected wallet. EIP-712 lets you present structured, human-readable signing requests so your users see exact intent. Throughout, I will emphasize safety: never ask for private keys, always validate input before sending to a contract, and handle network and account changes. By the end you will know concrete code patterns to connect wallets, request typed signatures, estimate gas costs, and present useful feedback to users. Think of this chapter as the bridge between smart contracts and a reliable, user-friendly frontend: it reduces surprises and improves security and trust for your users.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Advanced Web3 Frontend Integration
Advanced Web3 Frontend Integration & WalletConnect
Securely connect wallets, request typed-data signatures, and keep transactions reliable with clear feedback and gas-aware flows.
In this lesson
Provider vs Signer, WalletConnect integration, EIP-712 signing, gas estimation, and monitoring.
Why it matters
A robust integration prevents lost funds, reduces phishing risk, and supports more users across wallets and devices.
Explore Key Topics
Provider & Signer
Read-only queries use a Provider; sending transactions requires obtaining a Signer tied to a user's account.
WalletConnect
A protocol that connects your DApp to many wallets via a compatible provider usable by ethers.js or web3.js.
EIP-712 Signatures
Typed data signatures present clear intent to users and are safer than raw eth_sign messages.
Visual concept
BrowserProvider
Used for read-only calls and to request a signer when needed.
WalletConnect Provider
Acts as a bridge so the DApp can use a signer from many wallets.
Tip: Always present estimated gas and a clear description before requesting a transaction signature.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will apply when building DApps. First, you will master advanced contract interactions using ethers. js or web3. js: that means correctly choosing a provider for reads and a signer for writes and composing call and send flows. Second, you will implement multi-wallet support with WalletConnect and Web3Modal so users can connect via mobile wallets, hardware devices, or browser extensions. Third, you will learn complex signing patterns, including EIP-712 typed data signatures; this protects users by showing structured, human-readable signing requests. Fourth, you will develop robust error handling, accurate gas estimation, and transaction monitoring workflows so users see meaningful feedback during pending and confirmed states. Each objective is practical and testable: you will connect a wallet, sign a typed message, estimate gas for a sample transaction, and handle common errors like user rejection and insufficient funds. These capabilities reduce user friction and security risk and are the exact skills employers look for in production Ethereum frontends. As you progress, verify competency by completing hands-on tasks that replicate these production flows.

screens.title: How you will prove competency
screens.narratorSegment: To verify learning, you will complete short practical tasks that mirror production requirements. Demonstrate an ethers. js flow that reads token metadata using a Provider and then obtains a Signer to submit a state change; confirm the transaction receipt and show the emitted event. Implement Web3Modal with WalletConnect and connect at least two wallet types, observing account and chain change events. Create an EIP-712 signing sequence: prepare domain, types, and value objects, request a typed signature from the signer, and verify or send that signature to a relayer or contract for on-chain verification. Finally, add UI-side gas estimation and balance checks so that transactions are prevented when the user's balance cannot cover fees, and add targeted error messages for common codes like user rejection or insufficient funds. Each task is a clear milestone: a working read-write example, a successful WalletConnect session, a valid typed-data signature, and improved error reporting. These hands-on proofs ensure you can move from experimental code to production-ready integrations.

screens.title: ethers.js versus web3.js
screens.narratorSegment: When integrating a frontend with Ethereum, you will choose either ethers. js or web3. js. Both let you query the chain, call contracts, and sign transactions, but they differ in ergonomics and modern developer experience. Ethers. js is often preferred for a cleaner A P I surface, tighter TypeScript support, and straightforward provider and signer abstractions that separate read-only access from signing. Web3. js works well and is mature, but tends to have a broader historical A P I surface and different patterns for providers and subscriptions. A concrete example: with ethers. js you can create a BrowserProvider from window. ethereum, then call getSigner to sign transactions; the same flow exists in web3. js but the call signatures and return objects differ. One common misconception is that either library can magically prevent bad UX; they cannot. UX safety comes from how you use them: always estimate gas, check balances, and show clear prompts before signing. When you must support TypeScript-heavy codebases or want a compact, modern A P I, ethers. js is often the better choice. If you rely on legacy code or specific web3. js features, that library remains viable. The takeaway: pick the library that matches your team's needs, but implement the same safety patterns regardless of the choice.

keyIdea.title: Pick for ergonomics, not hype
keyIdea.text: Ethers.js offers modern APIs and TypeScript friendliness; web3.js is mature. Apply the same safety and UX patterns with either.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › ethers.js vs web3.js
Ethers.js (modern)
  • Cleaner API and modular packages.
  • Explicit Provider and Signer separation.
  • Strong TypeScript support and small footprint.
Common use: BrowserProvider + signer.getAddress() + contract.connect(signer)
web3.js (mature)
  • Long history and broad ecosystem plugins.
  • Different provider and subscription patterns.
  • Works well with many legacy projects.
Common use: web3.eth.* and provider objects tailored to dapp requirements
Key Takeaway

Choose a library for team ergonomics; always add gas checks, error handling, and clear signing prompts regardless of library.

Misconception
Neither library replaces careful UX design. Signing flows, gas estimation, and messaging still require explicit handling.
Example
Ethers example: create BrowserProvider, call getSigner, then contract.connect(signer) to send transactions.

screens.title: Provider and Signer
screens.narratorSegment: A Provider and a Signer play distinct roles in a DApp. The Provider gives read-only access to blockchain state: you use it to call view or pure contract functions or query balances and block data. The Signer represents a user's account and can sign transactions or typed data; it is necessary for any state-changing operation. Concretely, with ethers. js you might use a BrowserProvider to query a token's name and symbol, then call provider. getSigner() when the user clicks to submit a transfer. A common mistake is to hold a Signer when only reads are needed, which needlessly requires user consent. Another misconception is trusting getGasPrice alone; you should estimate gas for the specific call because contract logic can change gas use. Example: call tokenContract. name() with the provider to display metadata, then build a contract instance connected to the signer for transfer functions. For UI safety, read balances first, estimate gas for the intended transaction using contract. estimateGas. myFunction(...), compare estimated cost to the user's balance, and then request the signer to submit. The key takeaway: separate read and write flows, minimize the times you request a user signature, and always validate on the client before prompting the wallet.

keyIdea.title: Separation of concerns
keyIdea.text: Use Providers for reads and Signers for writes. Minimize sign requests and always validate and estimate before sending.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Provider & Signer
Definition
Provider: read-only interface to query chain state. Signer: an account capable of signing transactions or messages for state changes.
Concrete Example
import { ethers } from "ethers";

// Provider for reads
const provider = new ethers.BrowserProvider(window.ethereum);
const tokenContract = new ethers.Contract(tokenAddress, tokenAbi, provider);
const name = await tokenContract.name();

// Signer for writes
const signer = await provider.getSigner();
const myContract = new ethers.Contract(myContractAddress, myContractAbi, signer);
const tx = await myContract.setValue(123);
await tx.wait();
Practical Checklist
  • Read metadata with Provider; do not request signatures for reads.
  • Estimate gas before calling a write operation.
  • Show clear human-readable reason when requesting a signer action.
Misconception: A Signer is not a replacement for server-side validation; always validate inputs and handle reverts.

screens.title: Integrating WalletConnect & Web3Modal
screens.narratorSegment: Support for many wallets broadens your DApp's audience. WalletConnect provides a bridge that your frontend can consume through a wrapper UI like Web3Modal. The flow begins by configuring Web3Modal with a WalletConnect project ID and chain metadata, then calling a single open action to let the user choose their wallet. Once the user selects a wallet, Web3Modal yields a provider that is compatible with ethers. js or web3. js. Important practical steps: first, configure metadata including your DApp name and the chains you support. Second, create the Web3Modal instance so your UI has a consistent entry point. Third, on connection, wrap the returned provider into an ethers BrowserProvider or equivalent so your code can getSigner or perform reads as needed. Remember to subscribe to connection events and handle accountsChanged, chainChanged, and disconnect by updating application state. A common mistake is assuming WalletConnect connections persist like injected wallets; sessions can expire or be disconnected from the wallet side. Be ready to prompt reconnection and clear sensitive state on disconnect. This flow lets you support MetaMask, mobile wallets via QR, and hardware wallets through a unified integration path.

keyIdea.title: Multi-wallet strategy
keyIdea.text: Use Web3Modal + WalletConnect to provide a single integration surface that yields a provider usable by ethers.js for both reads and signed writes.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › WalletConnect Integration
Initialization Pattern
createWeb3Modal({
  ethersConfig: defaultConfig({ metadata }),
  chains: [mainnet],
  projectId,
  enableAnalytics: true
});

// Later, call open() to show the modal and get a provider
Note: Configure metadata and chain RPCs so wallets display correct chain and DApp info.
Connection Events
  • accountsChanged — update the user's address in your app state.
  • chainChanged — ensure the UI reflects the current chain and prompt if unsupported.
  • disconnect — clear sensitive state and require reconnection.
Misconception: WalletConnect behaves exactly like an injected wallet — treat it as a remote session that may disconnect at any time.

screens.title: Using ethers.js with a WalletConnect provider
screens.narratorSegment: After WalletConnect hands you a provider, you should convert it into the familiar ethers model so your existing code can reuse provider and signer patterns. The typical sequence is to receive the provider from Web3Modal, create an ethers BrowserProvider or JsonRpcProvider from it, and then call getSigner to request a signature. A concrete code walkthrough helps: obtain the walletProvider from Web3Modal, construct an ethers BrowserProvider with that walletProvider, and then use provider. getSigner() to sign typed data or send transactions. A common misconception is treating the returned provider as a raw RPC endpoint; instead, wrap it properly so methods like provider. waitForTransaction and signer. signTypedData work as expected. Also remember to subscribe to provider events so your app reacts to account and network changes. Finally, test with different wallet types — mobile WalletConnect sessions, desktop extensions, and hardware wallets — to ensure the provider surface behaves predictably. The code block below shows a simplified example for this conversion and sign usage so you can copy the pattern into your DApp. Using ethers.js with a WalletConnect provider means wrap the walletconnect provider into an ethers provider so existing provider/signer-based code works without change.. In practical terms, wrap the walletconnect session into an ethers-compatible provider and get a signer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Adapter pattern
keyIdea.text: Wrap the WalletConnect provider into an ethers provider so existing provider/signer-based code works without change.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Adapter: WalletConnect → ethers
Simplified conversion example
// After web3modal returns walletProvider
const ethersProvider = new ethers.BrowserProvider(walletProvider);
const signer = await ethersProvider.getSigner();

// Use signer for write operations and provider for reads
const myContract = new ethers.Contract(myContractAddress, myContractAbi, signer);
const tx = await myContract.setValue(123);
await tx.wait();
Example
This lets your existing contract code remain unchanged while supporting remote wallets.
Common Pitfall
Not handling disconnect events leaves stale addresses in your UI; always reset on disconnect.

screens.title: EIP-712 Typed Data Signatures
screens.narratorSegment: EIP-712 standardizes signing of structured data. Instead of signing a raw byte string, you build a domain, a set of types, and a value object. The wallet can then present a human-readable description of what the user is signing, including DApp name, chain ID, and the contract in question. This clarity significantly reduces phishing risk compared to generic eth_sign messages. A practical example is a Permit or GrantRole object; you include fields like owner, spender, value, nonce, and deadline so both the DApp and verifying contract know exactly what was approved. To implement this with ethers. js, create the domain, define the types, and pass a value object to signer. signTypedData. A common misconception is that EIP-712 is only for advanced flows; in fact, any off-chain approval or meta-transaction pattern benefits from typed data. The key steps are assembling the domain with your DApp name and the verifying contract address, declaring types that match your contract's expected struct, and passing the user's address and other fields in the value. The takeaway: prefer EIP-712 for any off-chain signature that will be interpreted or relayed on-chain.

keyIdea.title: Safer signatures
keyIdea.text: EIP-712 makes off-chain signing explicit and human-readable, reducing phishing risk and enabling verifiable meta-transactions.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › EIP-712 Typed Data
Concept
EIP-712 signs structured, typed data with domain separation so wallets can show readable intent to users.
Simplified pattern
const domain = { name: 'My DApp', version: '1', chainId: 1, verifyingContract: '0x...' };
const types = { Permit: [ /* fields */ ] };
const value = { owner: '0x...', spender: '0x...', value: ethers.parseEther('100'), nonce: 0, deadline: ... };
const signature = await signer.signTypedData(domain, types, value);
Practical Notes
  • Include chainId and verifyingContract to avoid replay across domains.
  • Match types to the contract struct so on-chain verification succeeds.
  • Show human-readable descriptions in the UI to reduce accidental approval.
Misconception: EIP-712 prevents all phishing. It helps, but attackers can still engineer convincing prompts; users and UI safeguards matter too.

screens.title: Gas Estimation Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Estimating gas before sending a transaction is essential to prevent failed or unexpectedly expensive transactions. Use contract. estimateGas. myFunction with the call parameters to approximate gas consumption for that specific call. Combine this with a current gas price or EIP-1559 fee estimates to compute a total gas cost. Then compare the required amount against the user's native balance. If the balance is insufficient, inform the user with a clear recommendation to top up rather than letting the wallet reject the transaction during confirmation. A concrete example is estimating gas for a token transfer, multiplying estimated gas by the current fee, and displaying an estimated cost in ETH to the user before requesting approval. A common mistake is relying on a default gas limit or ignoring EIP-1559 base and priority fees; network conditions change and you should fetch live fee estimates. Also be aware that estimateGas itself can fail if the transaction would revert; catch this and surface a helpful message explaining likely contract-level reasons. The key takeaway: proactive estimation and balance checks reduce user frustration and lower failed transaction rates.

keyIdea.title: Proactive safety
keyIdea.text: Estimate gas for the exact call, compute cost with live fees, and block submissions when the user's balance cannot cover fees.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Gas Estimation
Estimation Flow
  1. Call contract.estimateGas.myFunction(...) with identical parameters.
  2. Fetch current gas price or EIP-1559 fee estimates.
  3. Compute total estimated cost and compare to user balance.
  4. If insufficient, show an explanatory message and halt the request.
Key Takeaway

Proactively estimate gas and check balances to avoid rejected transactions and poor UX.

Common Error
Don't assume a static gas limit; contract complexity and network conditions change actual costs.

screens.title: Transaction Monitoring & Receipts
screens.narratorSegment: After sending a transaction, users expect clear feedback until the action is final. In ethers. js you can await tx. wait() to receive a TransactionReceipt once mined, or use provider. waitForTransaction to watch for confirmations. Provide explicit UI states such as pending with estimated confirmation time, confirmed with block and transaction hash, and failed with a human-readable error. For example, after calling myContract. someAction(...), display a pending state and periodically poll provider. getTransactionReceipt or rely on tx. wait(); when a receipt arrives, show confirmation, gas used, and any events parsed from logs. Consider offering links to external explorers if appropriate, but always display the essential information inside your app. A common misconception is that tx. wait() is synchronous and instantaneous; network latency and confirmation depth mean it can take time. Also, transaction replacement or reorgs can change outcomes; handle unexpected receipts by explaining next steps. Use event listeners to update UI when new blocks arrive and provide a graceful fallback to server-side services if you need faster or more reliable monitoring. The takeaway: monitoring makes transactions trustworthy; invest in clear states and recovery paths.

screens.title: Common Mistakes & Safety Notes
screens.narratorSegment: Security and UX mistakes are common when building DApp frontends, but they are avoidable with clear patterns. First, never ask users to reveal private keys; wallets manage keys for a reason. Second, avoid eth_sign for structured approvals—eth_sign signs raw bytes and can be misleading; prefer EIP-712 typed signatures for clarity. Third, handle network changes and disconnections: listen for chainChanged and accountsChanged events and update or clear app state so you do not show stale addresses. Fourth, do not embed A P I keys directly in frontend code when using third-party RPC providers; protect keys with environment variables or a proxy to avoid exposure. Fifth, do not present vague error messages; translate contract reverts and wallet errors into actionable advice. A common misconception is that signing once lets you skip subsequent checks; always validate inputs each time because contract state or allowances may change. The practical substitute is to estimate gas, verify balances, validate user input, and present structured prompts. The end result is a DApp that reduces fraud risk and improves user trust. screens.title: Putting it all together
screens.narratorSegment: To assemble a production-ready DApp frontend, combine the concepts from this chapter into a clear stack. Start with a light, read-only Provider that powers data queries and UI displays. On demand, obtain a Signer to perform writes or sign typed data. Use Web3Modal and WalletConnect to handle multiple wallet types through one user flow, ensuring your provider wrapping pattern supports both injected and remote providers. For any write path, estimate gas, check the user's balance, and show an explicit human-readable description of the action; if you're asking for a typed signature, use EIP-712 to include domain and contract context. After sending a transaction, monitor its state via tx. wait() or provider. waitForTransaction and present pending, confirmed, or failed states with clear next steps. Centralize error handling: map wallet and contract errors to helpful messages like "insufficient funds" or "transaction rejected." Finally, do not commit sensitive keys to the frontend; use secure backends for any server-side keys or relayer operations. This hierarchy—from provider to user prompts to monitoring—keeps your DApp reliable and user-trustworthy. Ask yourself after building: can a new user understand the prompt they will sign and recover from a failed transaction?

You will understand when to use a read-only provider versus a signer, how to add multi-wallet support so users can choose MetaMask, a mobile wallet, or hardware device, and why structured signatures like EIP-712 are safer than raw signing. We'll also cover practical patterns: estimating gas to avoid failed transactions, monitoring status until confirmation, and surfacing clear error messages. For example, you might use a BrowserProvider for reads, then obtain a signer when the user needs to submit a payable transaction. WalletConnect acts as a bridge for mobile wallets, enabling QR or deep-link connections instead of a single injected wallet. EIP-712 lets you present structured, human-readable signing requests so your users see exact intent. Throughout, I will emphasize safety: never ask for private keys, always validate input before sending to a contract, and handle network and account changes. By the end you will know concrete code patterns to connect wallets, request typed signatures, estimate gas costs, and present useful feedback to users. Think of this chapter as the bridge between smart contracts and a reliable, user-friendly frontend: it reduces surprises and improves security and trust for your users.

These objectives map to practical skills you will apply when building DApps. First, you will master advanced contract interactions using ethers. js or web3. js: that means correctly choosing a provider for reads and a signer for writes and composing call and send flows. Second, you will implement multi-wallet support with WalletConnect and Web3Modal so users can connect via mobile wallets, hardware devices, or browser extensions. Third, you will learn complex signing patterns, including EIP-712 typed data signatures; this protects users by showing structured, human-readable signing requests. Fourth, you will develop robust error handling, accurate gas estimation, and transaction monitoring workflows so users see meaningful feedback during pending and confirmed states. Each objective is practical and testable: you will connect a wallet, sign a typed message, estimate gas for a sample transaction, and handle common errors like user rejection and insufficient funds. These capabilities reduce user friction and security risk and are the exact skills employers look for in production Ethereum frontends. As you progress, verify competency by completing hands-on tasks that replicate these production flows.

Create an EIP-712 signing sequence: prepare domain, types, and value objects, request a typed signature from the signer, and verify or send that signature to a relayer or contract for on-chain verification. Finally, add UI-side gas estimation and balance checks so that transactions are prevented when the user's balance cannot cover fees, and add targeted error messages for common codes like user rejection or insufficient funds. Each task is a clear milestone: a working read-write example, a successful WalletConnect session, a valid typed-data signature, and improved error reporting. These hands-on proofs ensure you can move from experimental code to production-ready integrations.

When integrating a frontend with Ethereum, you will choose either ethers. js or web3. js. Both let you query the chain, call contracts, and sign transactions, but they differ in ergonomics and modern developer experience. Ethers. js is often preferred for a cleaner A P I surface, tighter TypeScript support, and straightforward provider and signer abstractions that separate read-only access from signing. Web3. js works well and is mature, but tends to have a broader historical A P I surface and different patterns for providers and subscriptions. A concrete example: with ethers. js you can create a BrowserProvider from window. ethereum, then call getSigner to sign transactions; the same flow exists in web3. js but the call signatures and return objects differ. If you rely on legacy code or specific web3. js features, that library remains viable. A Provider and a Signer play distinct roles in a DApp. The Provider gives read-only access to blockchain state: you use it to call view or pure contract functions or query balances and block data. The Signer represents a user's account and can sign transactions or typed data; it is necessary for any state-changing operation. Concretely, with ethers. js you might use a BrowserProvider to query a token's name and symbol, then call provider. getSigner() when the user clicks to submit a transfer.
